title: The Te Deum
hookLine: the Church's great hymn of thanks: we praise thee, O God
tomorrow: an old man holds a baby and says he's ready to go. why?

cards: The banquet at the end of a season. Somebody stands, taps a glass, and starts thanking people, and the room goes quiet. What do you sing when the whole journey's done?
For Catholics, one old answer is a Latin hymn named for its first two words, Te Deum. An old English version opens: "We praise thee, O God: we acknowledge thee to be the Lord."
A legend says Ambrose and Augustine made it up together at Augustine's baptism; scholars doubt it, but the legend stuck. And there's a real argument about when it belongs.

teach.h: SING IT ANYWAY: IT'S ABOUT GOD.
teach.b: Here's the question. A tradition has Catholics sing the Te Deum on the last day of the year, in thanks for the whole of it. But what about a year that was hard?
One side says: sing it anyway. Read the hymn, and it's barely about us. It's about God, praised by angels, apostles and martyrs, and all the earth.
Praise doesn't depend on how the year went, because it isn't a review of the year. It's a statement about who God is. That's a strong case, and it has carried people through terrible years.

The Church also prays the psalms of lament, the ones that ask how long and why. Singing thanks over a wound you haven't named can ring hollow, and God doesn't need you to pretend. Also a strong case, rooted in scripture.
Now look at how the Te Deum itself ends. After all that praise, it turns, and asks. In that same old English version: "O Lord, in thee have I trusted: let me never be confounded."
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Church's great hymn of thanks ends with a plea for help.
The thanks and the honesty live in one song.

how: Catholics sing or pray the Te Deum in the Office of Readings on Sundays and feasts, and by custom in thanksgiving on the last day of the year.

games.q: your family had a rough year: a job lost, a grandparent gone. on New Year's Eve your aunt starts the Te Deum. your cousin says, "thanks for what?" what's the best case for singing?
o: the year was secretly fine if you look closely.
praise is about who God is, and the hymn ends by asking.
you sing so the family doesn't feel awkward.
games.why: one side says praise doesn't depend on the year; the other warns against hollow thanks. the Te Deum holds both: praise, and then let me never be confounded.

practice: Count on your fingers five gifts from the road behind you: people, places, mornings, even a hard thing that taught you something. Fold each finger down as you name it.
If you pray, you can let the Te Deum's first line cover all five: we praise thee, O God.
